bigPicture: The pre-course is a **refresher** of high-school maths, not new material (reference: *Math Refresher to be Fit for the University*, E. G. De Giorgi).
Session 1 gives the **language** of every later definition: **propositions**, the five **logical operators**, **truth tables** and the **quantifiers** ∀, ∃.
Key surprise: **A ⇒ B is false only when A is true and B is false**.
The second half covers **sets**: notation, subsets, the **power set** (2ⁿ elements), operations ∪, ∩, \, complement, and **De Morgan's laws**.

concepts.name: Statements vs. propositions
concepts.simple: A proposition is a sentence that is clearly true or clearly false. ‘Zurich is the most beautiful city’ is just an opinion, so it is not one.
exam: **Definition:** a **proposition** is a sentence that is either **true or false, but never both**; its logical value (T or F) is its **truth value**.
- A **statement** may be subjective; a proposition is objectively true or false.
- **Simple** proposition: a single statement. **Compound** proposition: two or more propositions combined with logical operators; it still has **exactly one** truth value.
concepts.example: “St. Gallen is located in Switzerland” → proposition (true). “Zurich is the most beautiful city in the world” → not a proposition.

concepts.name: Logical operators and truth tables
concepts.simple: *Not* flips true/false; *and* needs both true; *or* needs at least one; *if…then* only fails when the ‘if’ part happens but the ‘then’ part does not; *if and only if* needs both to agree.
exam: | Name | Symbol | Reads as |
| Negation | ¬A | not A |
| Conjunction | A ∧ B | A and B |
| Disjunction | A ∨ B | A or B (**inclusive**) |
| Implication | A ⇒ B | if A then B |
| Equivalence | A ⇔ B | A if and only if B |
| A | B | A ∧ B | A ∨ B | A ⇒ B | A ⇔ B |
| T | T | T | T | T | T |
| F | T | F | T | T | F |
| F | F | F | F | T | T |
**Remark:** A ∨ B is the *inclusive* OR (true also when both hold); everyday speech often means exclusive OR – mathematics does not, unless stated.
concepts.example: A = “it rains” is false and B = “I take an umbrella” is true ⇒ A ⇒ B is **true** (vacuously true).

concepts.name: Implication: sufficient and necessary
concepts.simple: A promise ‘If Marc wins, Jane gives him a prize’ is only broken if Marc wins and gets nothing.
exam: - **A ⇒ B is only false when A is true and B is false.** If A is false the implication is automatically true (**vacuously true**).
- **Vocabulary:** for A ⇒ B, **A is sufficient for B**; **B is necessary for A**.
- From the exercise: **¬A ∨ B has exactly the same truth table as A ⇒ B** (they are logically equivalent).
concepts.example: A = “Marc wins the race”, B = “Jane gives Marc a prize”: Jane paying even though Marc lost does **not** break the promise.

concepts.name: Quantifiers and their negation
concepts.simple: ∀ means ‘for all’, ∃ means ‘there exists’. To negate ‘all are …’ you say ‘at least one is not …’.
exam: - **∀ : “for all”** (universal quantifier) · **∃ : “there exists”** (existential quantifier).
- ∀x ∈ ℝ, x² ≥ 0 (true) · ∃x ∈ ℝ : x² = 4 (true, e.g. x = 2).
- **Negation rules:** ¬(∀x, P(x)) ⇔ ∃x, ¬P(x) and ¬(∃x, P(x)) ⇔ ∀x, ¬P(x).
concepts.example: Negate “For every student x, x has passed the exam” → “There exists a student x who has **not** passed the exam.”

concepts.name: Not every sentence is a proposition (Liar paradox)
concepts.simple: ‘This sentence is false’ cannot be true or false without contradicting itself, so it is not a proposition.
concepts.exam: “This sentence is false” is **not a proposition**: it leads to a contradiction (the **Liar Paradox**) – it cannot consistently be assigned a single truth value.
concepts.example: If it were true, it would be false; if it were false, it would be true.

concepts.name: Sets: basic notions
concepts.simple: A set is a collection of different objects. You can list them {1, 2, 3, 4} or describe them by a rule.
exam: **Definition:** a **set** is a well-defined collection of distinct objects, called **elements**; x ∈ A if x belongs to A, x ∉ A otherwise.
- Describing a set: **by listing** A = {1, 2, 3, 4}; **by a defining property** A = {x ∈ ℕ : x ≤ 4}.
- Standard number sets: **ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ**.
- In “naive” set theory there is a **universal set Ω**; all sets A, B, … are collections of objects in Ω.
concepts.example: {x ∈ ℕ : x ≤ 4} lists the natural numbers up to 4 (with ℕ starting at 0 as in Session 2, this also includes 0).

concepts.name: Subsets, equality, empty set, power set
concepts.simple: A is inside B if every element of A is also in B. The power set is the set of all possible subsets; a set with n elements has 2ⁿ subsets.
exam: - **Subset:** A ⊆ B if ∀x, x ∈ A ⇒ x ∈ B.
- **Equality:** A = B ⇔ A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A.
- **Empty set** ∅ has no elements; **∅ ⊆ A for every set A**.
- **Power set** 𝒫(A): the set of **all** subsets of A. If A has n elements, **𝒫(A) has 2ⁿ elements**.
concepts.example: A = {1, 2}: 𝒫(A) = {∅, {1}, {2}, {1, 2}} – 2² = 4 elements (handwritten on the slide).

concepts.name: Set operations, Venn diagrams and De Morgan's laws
concepts.simple: Union = everything in either set; intersection = only what is in both; difference = in A but not in B; complement = everything outside A.
exam: | Operation | Notation | Meaning |
| Union | A ∪ B | {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B} |
| Intersection | A ∩ B | {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B} |
| Difference | A \ B | {x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B} |
| Complement | Aᶜ (in Ω) | {x ∈ Ω : x ∉ A} |
**De Morgan's laws:** **(A ∪ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ** and **(A ∩ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ**.
Venn diagram: A ∩ B is the overlapping region, A ∪ B everything covered by either circle; Aᶜ is everything in Ω outside A.

concepts.name: Combining logic and sets
concepts.simple: ‘and’ between conditions = intersection of the sets; ‘or’ = union.
exam: {x : P(x) ∧ Q(x)} = {x : P(x)} ∩ {x : Q(x)} and, analogously, {x : P(x) ∨ Q(x)} = {x : P(x)} ∪ {x : Q(x)}.
concepts.example: The power set of A = {1,2,3,4,5} has 2⁵ = 32 elements, e.g. ∅, {1}, {1, 2}.

connections: **Math A Lecture 1** repeats logic in more depth (exclusive OR, tautology, contradiction, proof by induction).
**Session 2:** the number sets ℕ ⊂ ℤ ⊂ ℚ ⊂ ℝ; **Session 3:** domains and ranges are sets.
The outline: “This is the language used to state every later definition – of a function, a limit, a derivative.”

questions: Build a truth table (e.g. ¬A ∨ B) and compare it with A ⇒ B.
Compute A ∪ B, A ∩ B, A \ B, Aᶜ and verify De Morgan.
Number of elements of a power set (2ⁿ).
Decide whether a sentence is a proposition.
traps: A ⇒ B is **true** when A is false.
Negation of “∀ … >” is “∃ … ≤” (both the quantifier and the inequality change).
∅ ⊆ A always; 𝒫(A) contains ∅ and A itself.
A is **sufficient** for B, B is **necessary** for A (not the other way round).
mistakes: Negating “all students passed” as “no student passed”.
Forgetting ∅ when listing a power set.

memorize: **A ⇒ B false only for A = T, B = F;** A ⇒ B ≡ ¬A ∨ B.
**De Morgan:** (A ∪ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ; (A ∩ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ.
**|𝒫(A)| = 2ⁿ;** A = B ⇔ A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A.

practice.question: When is A ⇒ B false?
practice.explanation: The implication is only false when A is true and B is false.

practice.question: A is true, B is true. What is A ∨ B?
Which proposition has the same truth table as A ⇒ B?
practice.explanation: ¬A ∨ B is logically equivalent to A ⇒ B.

practice.question: For A ⇒ B, which is correct?
practice.explanation: A sufficient for B; B necessary for A.

options: There exists a student who has not passed.
There exists a student who has passed.

practice.question: “This sentence is false” is…
practice.explanation: Liar paradox: no consistent truth value.

St. Gallen is located in Switzerland.

questions.question: A false, B false. Which is TRUE?
questions.explanation: A ⇔ B is true when both have the same value; A ⇒ B is true so its negation is false.

Which is NOT an element of 𝒫({1, 2})?
questions.explanation: Elements of the power set are sets; 1 is a number.

questions.question: Build the truth table of ¬A ∨ B and compare it with A ⇒ B. What do you observe?
questions.model:
A, B = TT: ¬A = F, ¬A ∨ B = T
TF: ¬A = F, ¬A ∨ B = F
FT: ¬A = T, ¬A ∨ B = T
FF: ¬A = T, ¬A ∨ B = T
A ⇒ B has the column T, F, T, T as well → ¬A ∨ B and A ⇒ B are logically equivalent.

keyPoints.text: All four rows with the correct ¬A column
Correct ¬A ∨ B column (T, F, T, T)
